This would be amazing if I could see it. I really hope the Moon is visible right now!

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 16:30 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T23:30:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 40.07 degrees and its azimuth is 254.785 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 46.927 degrees and its azimuth is 214.747 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 6.51 percent illuminated, 29.501 degrees from the Sun, and 372194.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—very likely.

The Moon is high in the southwest, at altitude **46.9°** and azimuth **214.7°** (roughly southwest), while the Sun is lower and farther west at azimuth **254.8°**. A **6.5%-illuminated crescent** can be visible in daylight when it is this high and separated from the Sun by about **29.5°**, especially under clear skies.

Look about **35° to the left of the Sun** as you face it—toward the south—and roughly **7° higher**. The crescent will be faint against the blue sky, so:

- Use the Sun only as a directional reference; **never look through binoculars or a telescope anywhere near it**.
- First locate it with unaided eyes, preferably by scanning slowly around the predicted position.
- A building, tree, or hat can shade your eyes from sunlight.
- It may be easier if you start from a known landmark or use the app’s sky view, but avoid letting the phone’s screen glare interfere.

Given the clear sky, high lunar altitude, and nearly 30° angular separation, an ordinary observer has a good chance—though the thin crescent may take patience and careful scanning.
